description: Stardust Crusaders it’s a team dedicated to monitoring human health while we do space exploration.
summary: TIRELUS is a health self-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions. It collects daily health indicators, compares each one with the astronaut's own preflight baseline and, when a deviation is sustained, tells the crew member what to do next and who to escalate to (astronaut → Crew Medical Officer → flight surgeon). A clickable body figure shows one status per system: heart, eyes (SANS), bone and muscle, sleep and mood, and immune. An environment selector (ISS, Moon, Mars) changes the communication delay and turns on an autonomous mode with deferred messages, because far from Earth the crew becomes its own first line of care. TIRELUS does not diagnose: it flags deviations, explains why each value changes in space and exports a private summary for the weekly medical conference. All data in the demo is synthetic.
details:
What it does.
TIRELUS helps each crew member check their own health between contacts with the ground:

  1. Main panel: a body figure with a status per system (heart, eyes/SANS, bone and muscle, sleep and mood, immune).
  2. Guided measurement: a step-by-step capture that compares the value with the personal preflight baseline and explains what it measures and why it changes in microgravity.
  3. Trend alert: a 14-day trend raises an alert only after a sustained deviation (3 consecutive days outside the baseline band), filtering one-off noise, and suggests a plan.
  4. Medical summary: exports a summary for the private weekly medical conference; a press-and-hold button notifies the CMO.
  5. ISS / Moon / Mars selector: changes the communication delay (Artemis round trip of 4–14 s; up to ~20 min each way to Mars) and activates an autonomous mode with a guided protocol, on-board decision options and delayed messages to the flight surgeon.

Extras: a base console (shared view without clinical data), plus helmet-visor and handheld concepts for EVAs. The whole interface works in English and Spanish.

How it works.

Three layers, all labeled as design assumptions:

  1. a personal baseline from preflight data (mean ± 2 SD of the first 14 days)-
  2. a sustained-trend rule.
  3. terrestrial clinical ranges as a backstop for "critical".

NASA does not publish in-flight alert thresholds for blood pressure, heart rate or lab values, so ours are design assumptions. The one published exception is SANS: a 2026 expert consensus sets +20 µm of peripapillary retinal thickness as the earliest sign and +55 µm or Frisén grade 1 as clinically concerning. Every status combines color, shape and word (nominal, attention, critical, no data) for color-blind readability, with text contrast of at least 4.5:1.

Architecture.

Flutter (Dart) interface → local HTTP API in Python (FastAPI + uvicorn) that holds the rules engine → PostgreSQL.

The app never talks to the database directly. If the database is unavailable, a built-in simulation of synthetic data keeps the app running. Logic is written once in Python and is designed to be embedded in the app with serious_python. The code is covered by 212 Python tests (pytest) and 126 Flutter tests. During the hackathon the team shared a PostgreSQL server holding synthetic data only; the final concept is an onboard PostgreSQL that works without Internet or a link to Earth.

Privacy.

Each crew member's medical data is visible only to that crew member, the CMO and the flight surgeon; shared screens never show clinical data.

Benefits and goals.

Earlier detection of slow changes, clear next steps when help is minutes away, and a consistent record for the medical team.

Next steps: save each new measurement on board so it feeds the trend in real time, turn the helmet-visor and handheld concepts into working EVA views, add the onboard database, and review thresholds with space-medicine experts.

Tools.
Flutter, Dart, Python, FastAPI, uvicorn, pg8000, pytest, PostgreSQL, serious_python.
